definitions.main_season_crop: It aims to represent the crop and cropping practices that are applied on cropland for more than 1/3 of a given cropping sequence, consistent with the classification of experimental data used to estimate default soil stock change factors
definitions.minor_season_crop: It represents crops and residue management practices applied for less than 1/3 of a given cropping sequence.
definitions.tillage_management: Tillage management refers to practices linked to the mechanical preparation and/or manipulation of soil and crop residues for the purpose of crop production.
definitions.cropland_input_level: Cropland input levels reflect practices affecting the amount of soil organic carbon in targeted land. They cover activities including, and not limited to, irrigation, soil cover, mulching, manure and fertilizer application, rotations, use of N-fixing crops.
definitions.crop_residue_management: Crop residue management refers to the handling of plant materials remaining in the field after harvesting.
definitions.definition_of_annual_cropland: Plants that perform their entire life cycle from seed to flower to seed, within a single growing season. All roots, stems and leaves of the plant die annually. Only the dormant seed bridges the gap between one generation and the next.
definitions.categories_of_tillage_management:
1. Full tillage: Substantial soil disturbance with full inversion and/or frequent (within year) tillage operations. At planting time, little (e.g., <30%) of the surface is covered by residues. 
2. Reduced tillage: Primary and/or secondary tillage but with reduced soil disturbance (usually shallow and without full soil inversion). Normally leaves surface with >30% coverage by residues at planting. 
3. No-till: Direct seeding without primary tillage, with only minimal soil disturbance in the seeding zone. Herbicides are typically used for weed control.
definitions.categories_of_input_organic_material:
1. Low carbon input: Defined by one of the following conditions:
•	Crop residues of annual crops are removed or burnt without using organic amendments (e.g. manure)
•	Low residue yielding crops are cultivated (e.g. cotton, green maize, vegetables, tobacco) or frequent rotation with bare fallow without organic amendments, cover crops/green manures, and mixed crop/grass systems.
•	Annual crops with no mineral fertilization or N-fixing crops without irrigation, cover crops/green manures, vegetated fallows, high residue yielding crops and mixed crop/grass systems.
2. Medium carbon input: Defined by one of the following conditions:
•	Annual cropping with cereals where all crop residues are returned to the field.
•	Crop residues of annual crops are removed or burnt BUT organic amendments (e.g. manure) are applied.
•	Low residue crops are cultivated or frequent rotation with bare fallow BUT using practices that increase C input above low residue varieties such as using organic amendments, cover crops/green manures, and mixed crop/grass systems.
•	Annual crops with no mineral fertilization or N-fixing crops BUT using practices that increase C input by enhancing residue production such as irrigation, cover crops/green manures, vegetated fallows, high residue yielding.
3. High carbon input without organic amendments:
•	The crop residues of annual crops are neither removed nor burnt. It represents significantly greater crop residue inputs over medium C input cropping systems due to additional practices, such as production of high residue yielding crops, use of green manures, cover crops, improved vegetated fallows, irrigation, frequent use of perennial grasses in annual crop rotations, but without manure applied.
4. High carbon input with organic amendments: 
•	Represents significantly higher C input over medium C input cropping systems due to an additional practice of regular addition of animal manure.
definitions.categories_of_crop_residue_management:
1. Residues retained: Crop residues are left on the field site to decompose and be re-incorporated in the crop's soil. Retaining of residues is usually associated with reduced or no-till practices.
2. Residues exported: Crop residues are removed from the field site, in order to be used for other activities (e.g. feeding, energy production).
3. Residues burnt: Crop residues are burnt

definitions.definition_of_perennial_cropland: It includes plants and other woody species that persist for many growing seasons. Generally the top portion of the plant dies back each winter and regrows the following spring from the same root system. It includes trees and shrubs, in combination with herbaceous crops (e.g., agroforestry) or as orchards, vineyards and plantations, except where these lands meet the criteria for categorisation as Forest Land.
definitions.categories_of_agroforestry_systems:
1. Fallows: Land rested from cultivation, but comprises planted and managed trees, often leguminous, shrubs and herbaceous cover crops before it is cultivated again. Includes improved and natural fallows, and can be implemented before any of the following systems.
2. Hedgerows: Linear plantation around fields, including shelterbelts, windbreaks, boundary plantings and live fences.
3. Alley cropping: Fast-growing, usually leguminous, woody species (mainly shrubs) grown in crop fields, usually at high densities. The woody species are regularly pruned and the prunings are applied as mulch into the alleys as a source of organic matter and nutrients. Also known as intercropping.
4. Multistrata systems: Multistorey combinations of a large number of various trees and perennial and annual crops. They include home gardens and agroforests.
5. Parklands: Intercropping of agricultural crops or grazing land under low density mature scattered trees. Typical of dry areas like Sahel (e.g. Faidherbia albida).
6. Shaded perennial-crop systems: Growing shade-tolerant species such as cacao and coffee under, or in between, overstorey shade trees that can be used for timber or other commercial tree products.
7. Silvoarable systems: Woody species planted in parallel tree rows to allow mechanization and intercropped with an annual crop; usually used for timber (e.p. Juglans spp), but also for fuel (e.g. Populus spp). Usually low tree density per hectare.
8. Silvopastoral systems: Woody species planted on permanent grasslands, often grazed.
9. Plantations [monoculture]: Monoculture plantation crops such as tea, coffee and cacao grown without shade trees, as well as oil palms, rubber and coconuts
10: Vine systems [monoculture]: A plantation of vines, typically producing grapes used for winemaking, but also kiwifruit or passionfruit
11: Orchard systems [monoculture]: Land planted with woody vegetation, often fruit trees (eg. apple, pear, plum, nut trees). Understory vegetation is usually mowed or grazed
12: Short rotation coppice [monoculture]: Fast-growing species of trees or other plant species grown on agricultural or forest land for a short period of up to eight years between two fellings or harvests for the purpose of producing high biomass yields for energy purposes.
13: Agroforestry-default: it represents a mathematical average of growth rates of all available agroforestry systems under the selected climate and moisture conditions.

definitions.cultivation_period: Refers to the number of days covered under each cropping season, from seeding to final harvest. The cropping seasons are set to 1 by default and can be up to 5. The sum of cultivation periods should never exceed 365 days, regardless of the number of cropping seasons.
definitions.definition_of_flooded_rice: Flooded rice refers to rice fields that are flooded for a significant period of time and the water regime is fully controlled. It refers to only flooded (permanently or part of the year), lowland rice fields. Non flooded rice, i.e. upland rice or pure rain-fed rice is considered an annual crop.
definitions.categories_of_organic_amendment:
1. Straw burnt: The practice of burning rice straw in the field after harvest.
2. Straw exported: The removal of rice straw from the field for use elsewhere, such as animal feed or biofuel production.
3. Compost: Organic matter that has been decomposed and recycled as a fertilizer and soil amendment.
4. Farm Yard Manure: A mixture of animal dung and urine with straw and litter used as bedding material, decomposed to varying degrees.
5. Green manure: e.g. Azolla. Azolla in association with blue-green alga anabaena can fix atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia which can be utilized by rice plant when it is incorporated into soil. Azolla contains from 2−5% N, 0.3−6.0% Potassium (K) (dry weight).
6. Straw incorporated shortly (<30 days) before cultivation: Straw applied just before rice transplanting as on-season; straw that is left on the soil surface in the fallow season and incorporated into the soil before the next rice transplanting is also categorized as 'straw incorporated shortly (<30 days) before cultivation'. The amount of straw return is expressed in dry weight (t ha-1). 
7. Straw incorporated long (>30 days) before cultivation: Straw incorporated into soils in the previous season (upland crop or fallow) is categorized as 'straw incorporated long (>30 days) before cultivation'. The amount of straw return is expressed in dry weight (t ha-1).
definitions.water_management_before_cultivation: Practices and strategies used to control water levels in rice fields during the pre-planting period. This includes managing the duration and timing of flooding or keeping the field dry before rice cultivation begins
definitions.water_management_during_cultivation: Practices used to control water levels in rice fields during the growing season, including both irrigated and rainfed systems.
definitions.categories_of_water_management_before_cu:
1. Flooded pre-season (>30 days): Permanently flooded rice fields are assumed to have a preseason water regime of 'flooded pre-season'. Late rice (e.g., in China) is usually planted immediately after early rice on the same field and is therefore regarded as having a pre-season water regime of 'flooded pre-season'. 
2. Non flooded pre-season (>180 days): If rice is planted once a year and the field is not flooded in the non-rice growing season, the preseason water regime is classified as 'non flooded pre-season >180 d'.
3. Non flooded pre-season (< 180 days): Rice is planted more than once a year, but there is more than one month of fallow time between the two seasons, 'non-flooded pre-season <180 d' usually implies pre-season drainage.
definitions.categories_of_water_management_during_cu:
a. Irrigated
1. Continuously flooded: Fields have standing water throughout the rice growing season and may only dry out for harvest end-season drainage. Rice is cultivated under continuously flooded condition but sometimes an end-season drainage before rice harvest included.
2. Single drainage: Fields have a single drainage event and period during the cropping season at any growth stage, in addition to the end of season drainage. One mid-season drainage and an end-season drainage are adopted over the entire rice-growing season.3. 
3. Multiple drainage: Fields have more than one drainage event and period of time without flooded conditions during the cropping season, in addition to an end of season drainage, including alternate wetting and drying (AWD). Also called 'intermittent irrigation', in which the number of drainage events was not clear, but there are more than one events during the growing season.

b) Rainfed and deep water
1. Rainfed, wet season (regular rainfed): Rice cultivation that relies on rainfall for water, in this case the field is flood prone during the rice-growing season. The water level may rise up to 50 cm during the cropping season.
2. Rainfed, dry season (drought prone): Rice cultivation that relies on rainfall for water, in this case the field is drought prone during the rice-growing season. Drought periods occur during every cropping season.
3. Deep water: Water level rises to more than 50 cm above the soil for a significant period of time during the cropping season.

definitions.grassland_management: Grassland management refers to the assessment and classification of grassland conditions based on its soil organic carbon stocks.
definitions.definition_of_grassland: Grasslands are generally defined by having vegetation that is dominated by perennial grasses, with grazing as the predominant land use.
definitions.definitions_of_fire_management:
1. Fire occurrence: Fire occurrence refers to the presence or absence of fire events in a given grassland area over the period of accounting. 
2. Fire periodicity: Fire periodicity describes the frequency or regularity of fire events in a grassland ecosystem. It is expressed as the average time (in years) between successive fire events. A value of 1 stands for 1 year between two fire events, a value of 2 stands for 2 years between two fire events.  
3. Fire impact: Fire impact refers to the effects of fire on the grassland ecosystem, expressed in the % of grassland biomass that is lost to each fire event.
definitions.categories_of_grassland_management:
1. Non-degraded: Represents non-degraded and sustainably managed grassland, but without significant management improvements. 
2. Moderately degraded / High intensity grazing: Represents high intensity grazing systems (or cutting and removal of vegetation) with shifts in vegetation composition and possibly productivity but is not severely degraded. Note: Termed "Moderately degraded" in IPCC 2006 and "High intensity grazing" in IPCC 2019. 
3. Severely degraded: Implies major long-term loss of productivity and vegetation cover, due to severe mechanical damage to the vegetation and/or severe soil erosion. 
4. Improved: Represents grassland which is sustainably managed with moderate grazing pressure and that receives at least one improvement: fertilization, species improvement, irrigation. 
5. Improved with high inputs: Applies to improved grassland where one or more additional management inputs/improvements have been used (beyond what is required to be classified as improved grassland).

definitions.manure_management: The term ‘manure’ is used collectively to include both dung and urine (i.e., the solids and the liquids) produced by livestock. Emissions accounted for include storage, digestion, pre-digestion, leakage and application to agricultural fields.The emissions associated with the burning of dung for fuel are to be reported under Energy activities. When manure is used in the production of biogas, the emissions reported under the manure management category are those occurring on the farm site not resulting from combustion.  Emissions from biogas combustion during the production of energy, whether on or off farm are to be reported under Energy activities.
definitions.productivity_systems: Productivity systems represent the production capacity of a specific set of livestock management practices. Default, high and low productivity systems may be defined according to characteristics such as: feedbase, genetics, purpose (draft, cultural reasons, self-consumption, market), production objectives (e.g. milk, meat, eggs), and level of inputs and outputs.
definitions.definition_of_livestock: Livestock are domesticated terrestrial animals that are raised to provide a diverse array of goods and services such as traction, meat, milk, eggs, hides, fibres and feathers.
definitions.categories_of_manure_management:
1. Pasture/Range/Paddock: The manure from pasture and range grazing animals is allowed to lie as deposited, and is not managed.
2. Daily spread: Manure is routinely removed from a confinement facility and is applied to cropland or pasture within 24 hours of excretion.
3. Solid storage: The storage of manure, typically for a period of several months, in unconfined piles or stacks. Manure is able to be stacked due to the presence of a sufficient amount of bedding material or loss of moisture by evaporation. 
4. Dry lot: A paved or unpaved open confinement area without any significant vegetative cover where accumulating manure may be removed periodically.
5. Liquid/Slurry: Manure is stored as excreted or with some minimal addition of water in either tanks or earthen ponds outside the animal housing, usually for periods less than one year.
6. Uncovered anaerobic lagoon: A type of liquid storage system designed and operated to combine waste stabilization and storage. Lagoon supernatant is usually used to remove manure from the associated confinement facilities to the lagoon. Anaerobic lagoons are designed with varying lengths of storage (up to a year or greater), depending on the climate region, the volatile solids loading rate, and other operational factors. The water from the lagoon may be recycled as flush water or used to irrigate and fertilise fields.
7. Pit storage below animal confinements: Collection and storage of manure usually with little or no added water typically below a slatted floor in an enclosed animal confinement facility, usually for periods less than one year.
8. Anaerobic digester: Animal excreta with or without straw are collected and anaerobically digested in a large containment vessel or covered lagoon. Digesters are designed and operated for waste stabilization by the microbial reduction of complex organic compounds to CO2 and CH4, which is captured and flared or used as a fuel.
9. Burned for fuel: The dung and urine are excreted on fields. The sun dried dung cakes are burned for fuel.
definitions.categories_of_productivity_systems:
1. Dairy cattle:
a) High-productivity systems:
     -High-yielding dairy cows that are concentrated in confinement production systems or grazing on high quality pastures with supplements.
     -The farms are 100-percent market oriented for commercial milk production, for national markets and/or export.
     -Purebred or crossbred cattle are genetically improved through selective breeding for milk production.
b) Low-productivity systems:
     -Low-yielding dairy cows, grazing non improved pastures, and using locally produced roughage (e.g. crop residues), and agro-industrial by-products.
     -Local breeds or crossbred cows are bred locally, without intensive selection for milk productivity.
     -Milk production is mostly for local market and local consumption.
2. Other cattle:
a) High-productivity systems:
     -Based on animal feeding systems using forage (e.g. high-quality grass) and concentrates in confinement production systems or grazing with supplements or on improved pastures, producing high rates of daily weight gain.
     -Animals can be purebred or crossbred and are genetically improved through selective breeding for improved commercial meat production.
     -Growing cattle may be finished young in "intensive grazing with supplements" or feedlot systems, and meat is produced for national markets and/or export.
b) Low-productivity systems:
    -Based on animal feeding systems where locally produced roughage (e.g. crop residues) or low quality rangelands represent the major source of feed utilized, poducing low rates of daily weight gain.
    -Animals can be represented by local breeds or may be crossbred and can also be used for multiple purposes such as draft, meat and milk for self consumption and markets.
3. For other livestock categories:
a) High-productivity systems:
    -Are 100 percent market oriented with high level of capital input requirements and high level of overall herd (flock) performance.
    -Feed is purchased from local or international market or intensively produced on farm.
    -Animals are improved through breeding practices for commercial production.
    -The high-productivity systems are common in swine, poultry, goats and sheep production.
b) Low-productivity systems:
    -Are mainly driven by local market or by self-consumption, with low capital input requirements and low level of overall herd (fowl) performance.
    -Typically using large areas for production or backyards.
    -Locally produced feed represents the major source of feed utilized or animals are kept-free range for major part or all of their production cycle, the yield of the activity being linked to the natural fertility of the land and the seasonal production of the pastures.
    -The low-productivity systems are common in swine, poultry, goats and sheep production.

definitions.categories_of_waterbodies:
Tidal freshwater pond: A pond or waterbody with  water column salinity < 0.5 parts per thousand (ppt). 
Canals and ditches: artificial structures conveying water inside or outside of a drainage area.
Brackishwater pond: A pond or waterbody with  water column salinity between 0.5 and 18 parts per thousand (ppt).
Saline pond: A pond or waterbody with  water column salinity between 0.5 and 18 parts per thousand (ppt).
definitions.definition_of_waterbodies: Water bodies include all flooded land where human activities have caused changes in the amount of surface area covered by water, typically through water level regulation.
definitions.categories_of_trophic_class:
1. Oligotrophic: An oligotrophic lake or reservoir is characterised by low primary productivity, as a result of low nutrient content. (Chl-a ≤ 2.6 µg L-1.)
2. Mesotrophic : A mesotrophic lake or reservoir is characterised with an intermediate level of productivity. (2.6 µg L-1 < Chl-a ≤ 20 µg L-1.)
3. Eutrophic : A eutrophic lake, pond or reservoir with high biological productivity. Due to excessive nutrients, especially nitrogen and phosphorus, these water bodies are able to support an abundance of aquatic plants. (20 µg L-1 < Chl-a ≤ 56 µg L-1.)
4. Hypereutrophic: A hypereutrophic body of water experiences the highest levels of biological productivity. (56 µg L-1 < Chl-a.)
5. Default:
definitions.definition_of_trophic_class: A measure of the biological productivity of a water body. It is usually characterized by some combination of nutrients, photosynthetic pigments (Chl-a) and/or water column optical properties. As the ambient nutrient levels increase, primary production (the algal population) increases and the water clarity decreases. As primary production increases, higher levels of biological production are supported and the trophic state increases.

definitions.gear_category:
Trawls: The trawl is a cone-shaped body of netting, usually with one codend, towed behind one or two boats to catch fish through herding and sieving.
Gillnets: Gillnets and entangling nets are long rectangular walls of netting that catch fish by gilling, wedging, snagging, entangling or entrapping them in pockets. These nets are kept open vertically by floats attached to the head rope (or float line, or cork line) and by weights added to the footrope, but they can also be held open vertically by hanging the net onto stakes.
Hooks and lines: Hook-and-line gears catch fish by the mouth with baited hooks, or by penetrating their flesh (impaling, ripping or tearing) with unbaited hooks when they pass within the range of movement of the hook. Bait can include natural bait fish or artificial lures.
Pots and traps: A pot is a small enclosure that attract fish through one or more entrances that allow the entry of fish but prevent or retard their escape. Traps are stationary structures of many shapes and sizes into which fish are guided, or pushed by the current, or drawn into the gear by bait or other attractants. 
Surrounding nets: A surrounding net is a long piece of net that is constructed mostly from rectangular sections of netting framed by ropes and catches fish by surrounding a school of fish.
Dredges: A dredge is a cage-like structure often equipped with a scraper blade or teeth on its lower part, either pulled or towed to dig animals out of substrate and lift them into the cage or bag.
definitions.categories_of_fisheries:
1. Small Scale Fisheries: These are characterised by a limited amount of production, taking place at a family or community level. They can be further defined by their limited (or lack of) fresh storage, close shoreline or short travel distance, smaller vessels, less-formally engaged economic activities, fewer crew, use of passive gears, among other characteristics. 
2. Large Scale Fisheries: Generally refers to fisheries at an industrial level, typically with vessels 12 metres in length or greater.
definitions.definition_of_fisheries: A Fishery is an activity leading to the harvesting of fish, within the boundaries of a defined area.

definitions.gear_category:
Bottom trawls:  The trawl is a cone-shaped body of netting, usually with one codend, towed behind one or two boats to catch fish through herding and sieving.
Gillnets and entangling nets. Trawls are designed to be towed across the seabed (bottom trawls) or in midwater (midwater trawls).
Hooks and lines: Hook-and-line gears catch fish by the mouth with baited hooks, or by penetrating their flesh (impaling, ripping or tearing) with unbaited hooks when they pass within the range of movement of the hook. Bait can include natural bait fish or artificial lures.
Midwater trawls: The trawl is a cone-shaped body of netting, usually with one codend, towed behind one or two boats to catch fish through herding and sieving.Trawls are designed to be towed across the seabed (bottom trawls) or in midwater (midwater trawls).
Gillnets and entangling nets: Gillnets and entangling nets are long rectangular walls of netting that catch fish by gilling, wedging, snagging, entangling or entrapping them in pockets. These nets are kept open vertically by floats attached to the head rope (or float line, or cork line) and by weights added to the footrope, but they can also be held open vertically by hanging the net onto stakes.
Traps and lift nets: Traps are stationary structures of many shapes and sizes into which fish are guided, or pushed by the current, or drawn into the gear by bait or other attractants. A lift net is a piece of netting mounted onto a frame that is lowered into the water to allow fish to enter the area above the net and is then lifted or hauled upward to collect the fish accumulated there.
Surrounding nets: A surrounding net is a long piece of net that is constructed mostly from rectangular sections of netting framed by ropes and catches fish by surrounding a school of fish.
Dredges: A dredge is a cage-like structure often equipped with a scraper blade or teeth on its lower part, either pulled or towed to dig animals out of substrate and lift them into the cage or bag.
Mobile Seine: A boat seine is a cone-shaped net with elongated wings, seine ropes and a codend, and operated by one or two boats, capturing fish by encircling and herding.

definitions.definition_of_aquaculture: Organised production of aquatic animals and plants (e.g. fish, crustaceans, and seaweeds) in marine or freshwater environments.

definitions.definition_of_settlements:
This category encompasses all developed land, including transportation infrastructure and human settlements of any size, unless already included under other categories. It can include:
1. Herbaceous perennial vegetation:
     - Turf grass (e.g., lawns and golf courses) 
     - Gardens
2. Trees in:
     - Rural settlements
     -Homestead gardens
     -Urban areas
3. Urban woodlands
4. Refuse areas (e.g., garbage dumps)
5. Barren areas (exposed soil)
6. Infrastructure:
     -Roadways
     -Houses
     -Buildings

definitions.forest_management: A system of practices for stewardship and use of forest land aimed at fulfilling relevant ecological (including biological diversity), economic and social functions of the forest.
definitions.categories_of_forest:
1. Primary Forest: A naturally regenerating forest of native tree species with no clear signs of human activities and minimal disturbance to ecological processes. This includes:
- Pristine and carefully managed forests for long-term conservation.
- Forests under traditional stewardship by Indigenous Peoples and local communities.
- Forests affected by natural disturbances.
- Excludes forests significantly impacted by hunting or gathering activities that have disrupted native species populations or ecological processes.

2. Secondary Forest: A forest composed of indigenous trees. It includes forests that are regenerating largely through natural processes after significant human and/or natural disturbance of the original forest vegetation at a single point in time or over an extended period, and displaying a major difference in forest structure and/or canopy species composition with respect to nearby primary forests on similar sites.It includes forests established through planting or seeding and under extensive management, which at stand maturity resembles or will resemble naturally regenerating forest. 

3. Forest Plantations (high density): Planeted forest that is intensively managed and meets all of the following criteria:  one or two species at planting, even age class, and regular spacing.
definitions.definition_of_rotations: Forest plantation rotations imply a periodic temporary biomass loss due to clearing of trees, and biomass gains over the rotation period due to replanting or assisted/natural regeneration.
definitions.categories_of_disturbance:
1. Disturbance by fire:Disturbance caused by wildfire regardless of whether it broke out inside or outside the forest. A wildfire is any unplanned and uncontrolled wildland fire which, regardless of ignition source, may require suppression response. 
2. Disturbance by diseases: Disturbances caused by diseases attributable to pathogens such as bacteria, fungi, phytoplasma, or virus. 
3. Disturbance by insects: Disturbance caused by insect pests that are detrimental to tree health. 
4. Other disturbances: Disturbance caused by factors other than fire, insects, or diseases. May include areas affected by drought, flooding, windfalls, acid rain, etc.
definitions.definition_of_disturbance: A disturbance is defined as an environmental fluctuation and destructive event that disturbs forest health, structure, and/or change resources or physical environment at any given spatial or temporal scale. Disturbances that affect health and vitality include biotic agents such as insects and diseases extreme
definitions.definition_of_timber_harvesting: Timber harvesting is the cutting and removal of trees, mainly for productive uses – for sale as timber or pulp, fuelwood, or for forest regeneration purposes. Timber harvesting activities include, and are not limited to, logging, thinning, fuelwood gathering. Timber harvesting through rotations should be represented in the "Rotation" section.

definitions.definition_of_other_land: Other land includes bare soil, rock, ice, and all land areas that do not fall into any of the other five categories.

definitions.definition_of_set_aside_land: Set aside land represents the temporary set aside of annually cropland (e.g., conservation reserves) or other idle cropland that has been revegetated with perennial grasses.

definitions.sources_of_energy:
Biodiesels: Liquid biofuels that are added to, blended with, or used straight as transport diesel. Examples: Biodiesel (methyl-ester from vegetable or animal oil), biodimethylether, Fischer Tropsch, cold pressed bio-oil.
Biogasoline: Liquid biofuels that are blended with or used straight as motor gasoline. Examples: Bioethanol, biomethanol, bioETBE, bioMTBE.
Charcoal: Solid residue of the destructive distillation and pyrolysis of wood and other vegetal material.
Gas/diesel oil: Includes heavy gas oils obtained from the lowest fraction from atmospheric distillation of crude oil to vacuum redistillation of the residual.
Jet kerosene: Medium distillate used for aviation turbine power units, with specific characteristics established by the International Air Transport Association (IATA).
Landfill gas: Gas derived from the anaerobic fermentation of biomass and solid wastes in landfills.
Liquefied petroleum gases (LPG): Light hydrocarbons of the paraffin series, derived from refinery processes, crude oil stabilization, and natural gas processing plants.
Lubricants: Hydrocarbons produced from distillate or residue, mainly used to reduce friction between bearing surfaces.
Motor gasoline: Light hydrocarbon oil for use in internal combustion engines, excluding aircraft.
Municipal wastes (biomass fraction): Biomass fraction of waste produced by households, industry, hospitals, and the tertiary sector, incinerated at specific installations for energy purposes.
Natural Gas: Includes natural gas and blended natural gas (sometimes referred to as Town Gas or City Gas).
Natural Gas liquids (NGL): Liquid or liquefied hydrocarbons produced in the manufacture, purification, and stabilization of natural gas.
Other biogas: Biogas not included in landfill gas or sludge gas.
Other kerosene: Refined petroleum distillate intermediate in volatility between gasoline and gas/diesel oil.
Other liquefied biofuels: Liquid biofuels not included in biogasoline or biodiesels.
Other petroleum products: Includes petroleum products not classified above, such as tar, sulphur, and grease.
Other primary solid biomass: Plant matter used directly as fuel, not included in wood/wood waste or sulphite lyes.
Paraffin waxes: Saturated aliphatic hydrocarbons with a crystalline structure and carbon number greater than 12.
Peat: Combustible soft, porous or compressed sedimentary deposit of plant origin with high water content.
Refinery gas: Non-condensable gas obtained during distillation of crude oil or treatment of oil products in refineries.
Residual fuel oil: Oils that make up the distillation residue, with specific physical characteristics.
Sludge gas: Gas derived from the anaerobic fermentation of biomass and solid wastes from sewage and animal slurries.
Sub-bituminous coal: Non-agglomerating coals with specific calorific value and volatile matter content.
White spirit & SBP (Special Boiling Point): Refined distillate intermediates with a distillation in the naphtha/kerosene range.
Wood/Wood waste: Wood and wood waste combusted directly for energy, including wood for charcoal production.

definitions.source_of_energy:
1. Motor Gasoline: Light hydrocarbon oil for use in internal combustion engines such as motor vehicles, excluding aircraft. Motor gasoline is distilled between 35ºC and 215ºC and is used as a fuel for land-based spark ignition engines.
2. Gasoil/Diesel oil: Includes heavy gas oils. Gas oils are obtained from the lowest fraction from atmospheric distillation of crude oil, while heavy gas oils are obtained by vacuum redistillation of the residual from atmospheric distillation. Gas/diesel oil distils between 180ºC and 380ºC.
3. Waste oil/Lubricants: Hydrocarbons produced from distillate or residue; they are mainly used to reduce friction between bearing surfaces. This category includes all finished grades of lubricating oil, from spindle oil to cylinder oil, and those used in greases, including motor oils and all grades of lubricating oil base stocks.
4. LPG (Liquefied Petroleum Gas): Light hydrocarbons fraction of the paraffin series, derived from refinery processes, crude oil stabilization plants and natural gas processing plants comprising propane (C3H8) and butane (C4H10) or a combination of the two. They are normally liquefied under pressure for transportation and storage.
5. Natural Gas: Should include natural gas and blended natural gas (sometimes referred to as Town Gas or City Gas), a high calorific value gas obtained as a blend of natural gas with other gases derived from other primary products, and usually distributed through the natural gas grid.
6. Electricity: Refers to electrical energy used to power irrigation pumps and systems.
7. Solar: Energy derived from solar radiation, often through photovoltaic panels, used to power irrigation systems.
definitions.categories_of_irrigation:
1. Surface without IRRS: Surface irrigation without an irrigation runoff return system.
2. Surface with IRRS: Surface irrigation with an irrigation runoff return system.
3. Solid set sprinkler: Irrigation with vertical tubes that are stationary for the duration of the irrigation season.
4. Permanent sprinkler: Irrigation with vertical tubes that cannot be moved from the moment they are installed.
5. Hand moved sprinkler: Irrigation with sprinklers that can be displaced throughout the irrigation season.
6. Solid roll sprinkler: An aluminum sprinkler line mounted on wheels which irrigates in place.
7. Center pivot sprinkler: Overhead sprinkler irrigation consisting of several segments of pipe, with sprinklers positioned along their length, joined together and supported by trusses, and mounted on wheeled towers.
8. Traveler sprinkler: Fully movable irrigation system that does not entail the construction of any stable irrigation infrastructure on the field.
9. Trickle: High precision, high efficiency drip irrigation.

definitions.drainage: Drainage of wetlands refers to the artificial lowering of the soil water table and removal of surface water from wetlands by gravity or pumping. This is typically done through the construction of drainage ditches, pipes, or tiles to redirect water away from the wetland area. The purpose is often to make the land suitable for agriculture, forestry, or urban development.
definitions.definition_of_organic_soil:
Soil that satisfies the requirements 1 and 2, or 1 and 3 below: 
1) Thickness of organic horizon greater than or equal to 10 cm. A horizon of less than 20 cm must have 12 percent or more organic carbon when mixed to a depth of 20 cm; 
2) Soils that are never saturated with water for more than a few days must contain more than 20 percent organic carbon by weight (i.e. about 35 percent organic matter); and 
3) Soils are subject to water saturation episodes and have either: 
     a) At least 12 percent organic carbon by weight (i.e. about 20 percent organic matter) if the soil has no clay; or
     b) At least 18 percent organic carbon by weight (i.e. about 30 percent organic matter) if the soil has 60% or more clay; or 
     c) An intermediate proportional amount of organic carbon for intermediate amounts of clay.

definitions.categories_of_vegetation:
Mangrove: Mangroves are salt-tolerant evergreen trees and shrubs growing in intertidal environments at the land–sea interface along tropical and subtropical coastlines, shallow-water lagoons, estuaries, rivers and deltas. 
Tidal marsh: Tidal marsh is a largely herbaceous community that occurs in the portion of the coastal zone affected by tides and seawater and protected from large waves, either by the broad, gently sloping topography of the shore or by a barrier island.
Seagrass: Flowering plants that  live underwater and grow in sediment on the sea floor with erect, elongate leaves and a buried root-like structure.
definitions.excavation_(_extraction):
Excavation collectively refers to:
1. Excavation of saturated soils leading to unsaturated (drained) soils and removal of biomass and dead organic matter. Activities that lead to the excavation of soil often lead to loss of coastal wetlands. The excavated or dredged soil is also commonly used to help develop coastal infrastructure where there is a need to raise the elevation of land in low lying areas and/or contribute to new land areas for settlement.
2. Excavation during the "construction" phase of aquaculture and salt production ponds in mangroves and tidal marshes followed by the "use" of these facilities.
definitions.definition_of_coastal_wetlands: Coastal wetlands generally consist of organic and mineral soils that are covered or saturated, for all or part of the year, by tidal freshwater, brackish or saline water and are vegetated by vascular plants. The boundary of coastal wetlands may extend to the landward extent of tidal inundation and may extend seaward to the maximum depth of vascular plant vegetation.
definitions.rewetting_and_revegetation_(_restored_ve:
The deliberate action of changing a drained soil into a wet soil, e.g. by blocking drainage ditches, disabling pumping facilities or breaching obstructions.
The rewetting and revegetation activity refers collectively to the following
1. Rewetting, which saturates the soil of drained sites previously colonised by mangrove and tidal marshes and is a prerequisite for, and thus facilitates, reestablishment of the original vegetation by natural recolonisation, direct seeding and/or purposeful planting.
2. Raising or lowering the soil elevation to facilitate reestablishment of the original vegetation by natural recolonisation, direct seeding and/or purposeful planting. 
3. Creation of coastal wetlands where it may be difficult to identify where they previously occurred and are in proximity to the coastal margin. 
4. Reestablishment of seagrass on undrained soils by natural recolonisation, direct seeding and/or purposeful planting.

definitions.categories_of_land_use:
1. Forest: A minimum area of land of 0.5 – 1.0 hectares with tree crown cover (or equivalent stocking level) of more than 10 – 30 per cent with trees with the potential to reach a minimum height of 2 – 5 meters at maturity in situ. In EX-ACT, the category includes natural forests and forest plantations.
3. Annual cropland: Plants that perform their entire life cycle from seed to flower to seed, within a single growing season. All roots, stems and leaves of the plant die annually. Only the dormant seed bridges the gap between one generation and the next. Selected, non woody pluriannual species are also included in this category (e.g. sugarcane) whenever their growth implies a harvest cycle for the entire plant.
4. Perennial cropland (agroforestry): It includes plants and other woody species that persist for many growing seasons. Generally the top portion of the plant dies back each winter and regrows the following spring from the same root system.
5. Flooded rice: It refers to only flooded (permanently or part of the year), lowland rice fields. Non flooded rice, i.e. upland rice or pure rain-fed rice is considered an annual crop.
6. Set aside: Set aside land represents land that is temporary set aside from annual crop production (e.g., conservation reserves) or other idle cropland that has been revegetated
7. Grassland: Grasslands are generally defined by having vegetation that is dominated by perennial grasses, with grazing as the predominant land use. This category includes rangelands and pasture land that are not considered Cropland. It also includes systems with woody vegetation and other non-grass vegetation such as herbs and brushes that fall below the threshold values used in the Forest Land category. The category also includes all grassland from wild lands to recreational areas as well as agricultural and silvi-pastural systems, consistent with national definitions.
8. Settlements:This category includes all developed land, including transportation infrastructure and human settlements of any size, unless they are already included under other categories. It includes soils, herbaceous perennial vegetation such as turf grass and garden plants, trees in rural settlements, homestead gardens and urban areas.
9. Wetlands:This category includes areas of peat extraction and land that is covered or saturated by water for all or part of the year (peatlands and other wetland types) and that does not fall into the Forest Land, Cropland, Grassland or Settlements categories. It includes reservoirs as a managed sub-division and natural rivers and lakes as unmanaged sub-divisions.
10. Degraded land: Degraded lands are those whose native vegetation has been heavily disturbed. The land has strongly degraded biomass and soil organic carbon levels.
11. Other land: This category includes bare soil, rock, ice and all land areas that do not fall into any of the other categories.
definitions.definition_of_land_use_change: A land use change is defined as the process of transformation incurring when land under a specific use is converted for different purposes. It is dependent on land use definitions provided below

definitions.categories_of_inputs:
Fertilizers: The term fertilizer refers to a chemical or natural substance or material that is used to provide nutrients to plants, usually via application to the soil, but also to foliage or through water in rice systems, fertigation or hydroponics or aquaculture operations. Thus, multiple nutrient types and sources are considered and include: chemical and mineral fertilizers; organic fertilizers such as livestock manures and composts; and sources of recycled nutrients such as wastewater, sewage sludge, digestates and other processed wastes.
Pesticides: A pesticide is defined as a natural or synthetic substance used for controlling or modifying plant growth processes without reducing nutritive value or causing severe phytotoxicity.
Animal feed: Animal feed refers to any raw or processed product given to farm animals in the course of husbandry or production processes. It includes both livestock and aquaculture feeds.
definitions.definition_of_inputs: Inputs include all resources used during farm processes that can support production. In EX-ACT, they include fertilizers, pesticides and animal feed.
definitions.fertilizer_categories:
Lime application: Liming is the addition of carbonates to soils in the form of calcic limestone or dolomite, which lead to CO2 emissions from carbonate dissolution.
Synthetic fertilizers: Synthetic or inorganic fertilizers included all products obtained by chemical processes, mineral extraction or by mechanical grinding. Note that though urea is technically an organic material, it is referred as an inorganic fertilizer  in line with the FAO fertilizer code.
N-fertilizers on irrigated rice: It includes the use of nitrogen based fertilizers on irrigated rice. Since nitrogen emissions are significantly dependent on moisture conditions and use in dry or wet land, the category is presented in a dedicated section.
Organic N-fertilizers: Organic fertilizers are derived from organic materials, including treated or untreated livestock manures, compost, vermicompost, sewage sludge and other organic materials or mixed materials used to supply nutrients
